query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: Enhancing the degree of local chemical order (LCO) in multi-element near‐equiatomic solid‐solution nanoparticles via an optimized post‐synthesis thermal treatment (extended annealing followed by rapid quenching) improves their structural and chemical stability under high-temperature catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) operating conditions, even with low noble-metal content.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles synthesized by conventional physical or chemical methods that yield a largely random, minimally ordered chemical structure.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled post-synthesis thermal treatment involving extended annealing at elevated temperatures to promote atomic ordering, followed by rapid quenching to lock in the enhanced local chemical order.
generation.conditions: Testing under simulated high-temperature catalysis (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric operation (473–1923 K) in controlled laboratory environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of local chemical order (LCO) within the nanoparticle lattice, as measured by high-resolution TEM and synchrotron X-ray diffraction.
generation.mechanism: Optimized thermal treatment promotes enhanced LCO, which raises the migration energy barriers for defect formation and atomic diffusion. This reduction in defect mobility suppresses coarsening, phase separation, and oxidation, thereby stabilizing both the structure and the chemical composition of the nanoparticles under harsh service conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles subjected to the enhanced thermal treatment will exhibit significantly slower coarsening, better phase integrity, and improved retention of chemical homogeneity compared to untreated nanoparticles when exposed to high-temperature operational conditions.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles produced with standard post-synthesis processing that do not intentionally enhance LCO, resulting in a more random chemical structure.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold for near-equiatomic, multi-element solid-solution nanoparticles under the specified high-temperature ranges; outcomes may vary with different elemental compositions or service conditions outside the provided temperature windows.
generation.uncertainty: While prior evidence supports the role of LCO in stabilizing the structure, the exact quantitative improvements and potential influences of additional factors (e.g., impurities or support interactions) remain uncertain until empirically validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical multi-element near-equiatomic nanoparticles. Subject one set to standard post-synthesis processing (baseline) and the other set to extended annealing with rapid quenching to enhance LCO. Expose both sets to controlled high-temperature environments replicating catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) conditions. Monitor their structural and chemical evolution in real time.
measurements: In situ TEM to track particle coarsening and morphological changes.
Synchrotron XRD to quantify the degree of LCO and phase integrity.
EDS mapping to assess chemical homogeneity over time.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles treated to enhance LCO do not show statistically significant improvements in structural integrity (e.g., reduced coarsening, maintained phase stability) and chemical homogeneity compared to the baseline nanoparticles under identical high-temperature conditions, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy oxides (HEOs) have aroused growing interest due to fundamental questions relating to their structure formation, phase stability, and the interplay between configurational disorder and physical and chemical properties. Introducing Fe(II) and Mn(II) into a rocksalt HEO is considered challenging, as theoretical analysis suggests that they are unstable in this structure under ambient conditions. Here, we develop a bottom-up method for synthesizing Mn- and Fe-containing rocksalt HEO (FeO-HEO). We present a comprehensive investigation of its crystal structure and the random cation-site occupancy. We show the improved structural robustness of this FeO-HEO and verify the viability of an oxygen sublattice as a buffer layer. Compositional analysis reveals the valence and spin state of the iron species. We further report the antiferromagnetic order of this FeO-HEO below the transition temperature ~218 K and predict the conditions of phase stability of Mn- and Fe-containing HEOs. Our results provide fresh insights into the design and property tailoring of emerging classes of HEOs. Bulk materials have very low dispersion, i.e., a low ratio of surface to bulk atoms. A large surface-to-bulk atom ratio is, however, vital for efficient catalysts. Nanoparticles possess such high dispersion. This generates a large interest in developing HEA nanoparticle synthesis methods. Many synthesis methods for HEA nanoparticles are high-energy shock methods such as Joule-heating, microwave heating, laser-ablation, and fast-bed pyrolysis. Recent studies propose that it is also possible to use low-temperature solution-based techniques to synthesize HEA nanoparticles or low-temperature reduction of solid precursors. Such methods open for fine-tuning both the composition and nanostructure of nanoparticles. For high-temperature synthesis approaches, entropy plays a role in stabilizing the multi-metallic phases, so that single-phase materials can be prepared. Thermal shock methods are also believed to freeze the material in a state of high entropy during controlled cool-down. The stability of the MEA-NPs is critical for their practical application at elevated temperatures. We, therefore, performed an in situ stability test in the electron microscope from room temperature up to 873 K, annealing the NPs at each test point for at least 30 min. As shown in Fig. 4A, the ultrafine Ru-5 MEA-NPs maintain their uniform dispersion throughout the in situ tests up to 873 K and demonstrate superior size stability after high-temperature annealing. In addition, the NPs are still in a homogeneous alloy structure without elemental segregation or phase separation (Fig. 4B), showing their structural stability. Note that the Co and Ni after annealing are slightly less than the nominal composition, which is likely due to metal evaporation at high temperature in the microscope vacuum. We also confirmed the alloy structure macroscopically by powder and synchrotron x-ray diffraction, showing a single-phase fcc structure with a fitted lattice constant of 3.673 Å (fig. S3, B and C).

decision.trend: Early studies used atomistic simulations (e.g., PMC6687833, PMC6820750) to reveal that local chemical order (LCO) in multi-principal element alloys not only affects dislocation pathways but also modulates energy barriers in deformation. Later work (PMC8797181) demonstrated that driving a disorder-to-order transition via rapid thermal interventions can produce ultrasmall, structurally stable multi-element nanoparticles. More recent studies (PMC10104586) have begun to show that LCO can also influence defect dynamics under external stresses (like irradiation), suggesting that the degree of chemically ordered motifs may be key to stability under harsh conditions. However, despite these insights, a quantitative synthesis–structure–property map that links controlled thermal processing to the degree of LCO, and in turn to stability under high-temperature service conditions, remains unresolved.
decision.unsolved: The core unsolved issue is how variations in local chemical order (arising from different synthesis/thermal treatments) govern the structural and chemical stability of near-equiatomic, multi-element nanoparticles under high-temperature catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) conditions. In particular, it is unclear whether manipulating post-synthesis thermal treatments can reliably enhance service stability, especially when low noble-metal content is desired, and what quantitative markers (e.g., degree of LCO) will correlate with improved performance.
decision.lever: systematically vary post-synthesis thermal treatments—specifically, tuning annealing durations and quenching rates to modulate the extent of local chemical order across nanoparticles
decision.why: Prior evidence indicates that LCO plays a critical role in determining dislocation dynamics and defect stability in multi-element alloys. A controlled experiment that adjusts thermal treatments provides a clear lever to vary LCO levels. By subjecting these treated nanoparticles to simulated high-temperature catalysis and thermoelectric conditions and tracking structural and chemical stability (e.g., via in situ advanced characterization), researchers can directly test the hypothesis that enhanced LCO correlates with superior stability. Observations deviating from the predicted enhanced stability under increased LCO (i.e., similar or decreased stability) would directly falsify the hypothesis, thereby isolating the mechanistic role of LCO in service performance.
